taxonomy.title: Anorectal — anal HSIL and cancer
taxonomy.scopeIn: Anal HSIL/HPV, anal-canal and margin neoplasia, tissue diagnosis, local/distant staging, chemoradiation response and salvage decisions.
taxonomy.scopeOut: Rectal adenocarcinoma belongs to colorectal-polyps-cancer. Benign fistula and fissure belong to anorectal-benign-pelvic-floor.
taxonomy.priorityReason: A distinct disease pathway prevents mixing anal and rectal staging or treatment.
taxonomy.coverageReason: At most four distinct live clinical concept identities cover this scope. Variants repeat those identities.
taxonomy.testingWeightBasis: Owner-directed editorial estimate of general-surgery testing relevance. No exam percentages or official blueprint weights are asserted.

recordedHolds.reason: Initial chemoradiation recognition is already covered; a response-versus-salvage decision needs a clinician-endorsed timing boundary.
recordedHolds.ownerQuestion: At eight weeks after anal-cancer chemoradiation, if the lesion is steadily shrinking but a small ulcer remains without progressive findings, should the key be repeat response assessment rather than abdominoperineal resection?

items.value: Lesion centered within the anal canal rather than on the perianal skin; continence preserved.

items.label: CT chest/abdomen/pelvis
items.value: No distant metastasis identified.

answerChoices.label: Definitive combined chemoradiation
answerChoices.rationale: The anal-canal squamous primary remains nonmetastatic on completed staging. Sphincter involvement does not by itself convert it to a rectal-cancer resection problem; definitive chemoradiation is the supported broad initial path.

answerChoices.label: Abdominoperineal resection
answerChoices.rationale: This gives sphincter involvement an automatic operative consequence rather than applying the anal-canal squamous treatment pathway.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This gives sphincter involvement an automatic operative consequence rather than applying the anal-canal squamous treatment pathway.

answerChoices.label: Transanal local excision
answerChoices.rationale: The lesion's canal origin and represented sphincter extent are not a limited superficial local-lesion problem suited to this proposed operation.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The lesion's canal origin and represented sphincter extent are not a limited superficial local-lesion problem suited to this proposed operation.

question.explanation: The completed assessment shows an anal-canal squamous primary without distant spread. The correct initial broad pathway is definitive chemoradiation, despite local sphincter involvement. Radical rectal-type surgery and limited transanal excision arise from different readings of the site and extent. No chemotherapy agents, radiation dose, staging cutoff or salvage indication is newly prescribed.

rankedConcepts.title: Regional disease versus metastatic treatment intent
rankedConcepts.decision: Choose the initial treatment pathway after locating nodal spread.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Anal-canal squamous histology, inguinal-node sample, distant CT and local MRI.
rankedConcepts.closestError: Call an inguinal node distant disease or import a rectal-resection rule.
rankedConcepts.consequence: Wrong cancer-treatment intent instead of standard curative local-regional care.
rankedConcepts.coverage: Four redundant live initial-treatment variants; one raw-distribution rewrite.
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: Core surgery oncology decision; ranking is qualitative editorial judgment, not exam-frequency data.

rankedConcepts.title: Representative tissue and specimen provenance
rankedConcepts.decision: Decide which current lesion still needs diagnostic tissue.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Procedure map, specimen label, examined target and conflicting negative screening.
rankedConcepts.closestError: Apply benign wrong-site tissue or a negative swab to an unsolved palpable lesion.
rankedConcepts.coverage: Four supplied-workup live variants; one rewrite plus one consequential negative-screen variant using the same stable identity.
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: Frequent practical reasoning error transferable across colorectal cases.

rankedConcepts.title: Regression versus progression after chemoradiation
rankedConcepts.decision: Distinguish slow response from failure before biopsy or salvage.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Serial examinations, treatment initiation and completion dates, ulcer trajectory and new progressive findings.
rankedConcepts.closestError: Call a shrinking early residual ulcer treatment failure.
rankedConcepts.consequence: Premature radical treatment or delayed response evaluation.
rankedConcepts.coverage: No scored response item. Existing owner hold remains unkeyed.
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: High-value gap, specifically requested by earlier review; exact timing clock needs Melissa.

rankedConcepts.title: Confirmed isolated local failure and salvage APR
rankedConcepts.decision: Confirm viable recurrence and choose the salvage pathway after restaging.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Prior complete response, new scar nodule, representative biopsy, prior radiation and resection planes.
rankedConcepts.closestError: Treat imaging as tissue proof or equate any recurrence with metastatic disease.
rankedConcepts.consequence: Unjustified radical surgery or missed curative salvage opportunity.
rankedConcepts.coverage: Previously absent; new two-node clinic record-review case.
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: Consequential operation selection with distinct diagnostic and treatment phases.

rankedConcepts.title: Canal versus margin, differentiation and clearance
rankedConcepts.decision: Select postoperative care after a skin-margin SCC excision.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Operative site map, differentiation, measured clearance and nodal assessment.
rankedConcepts.closestError: Apply blanket canal CRT or use negative margins to ignore adverse differentiation.
rankedConcepts.coverage: Previously absent. Two independent opposite-key siblings share one new construct; close-margin management remains unkeyed.
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: Commonly testable exception to the main anal-cancer pathway, with a consequential histologic discriminator.

rankedConcepts.title: Abnormal cytology versus tissue diagnosis
rankedConcepts.decision: Arrange directed histology despite normal palpation.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Swab cytology, HPV result, physical examination and actual prior specimen history.
rankedConcepts.closestError: Repeat screening or stage an unproven invasive cancer.
rankedConcepts.consequence: Missed precursor or incorrectly inferred cancer diagnosis.
rankedConcepts.coverage: No existing scored diagnostic HSIL pathway; new first node.
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: Practical screening-to-diagnosis transition, not viral association recall.

rankedConcepts.title: Treat confirmed anal HSIL in adults with HIV
rankedConcepts.decision: Choose lesion treatment instead of monitoring or cancer therapy.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Epithelial architecture, represented stroma, HIV context and accessible focal lesions.
rankedConcepts.closestError: Equate no invasion and HIV suppression with no treatment indication.
rankedConcepts.consequence: Leave a treatable precursor untreated or overtreat with cancer therapy.
rankedConcepts.coverage: Previously only HPV-cause recall; new management node.
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: Current evidence changes a real decision; do not claim modality superiority or extrapolate ANCHOR to every population.

rankedConcepts.title: Usable local staging versus completed distant staging
rankedConcepts.decision: Resolve the correct staging information gap.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: CT scope plus separate acquisition, archive and export records.
rankedConcepts.closestError: Repeat a completed acquisition or substitute metabolic imaging for local anatomy.
rankedConcepts.consequence: Unnecessary testing or incomplete treatment planning.
rankedConcepts.coverage: Retained N3 v1 rewritten with the same meaning and a new exact question.
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: Acquisition adequacy and local/distant scope are clinically actionable; no inconsequential stage-label objective.

rankedConcepts.title: Previously irradiated isolated groin recurrence
rankedConcepts.decision: Choose regional rather than primary-site salvage.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Current biopsy, control of the canal primary, distant staging and archived groin field.
rankedConcepts.closestError: APR for every recurrence or re-treat an irradiated groin automatically.
rankedConcepts.consequence: Wrong target or wrong radiation-field assumption.
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: Harder specialist-adjacent decision still within surgical oncology scope; evidence is consensus-heavy.

rankedConcepts.title: Metastatic first-line versus post-platinum therapy
rankedConcepts.decision: Read the actual earlier drugs before selecting a systemic pathway.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Biopsy-matched disseminated recurrence and prior fluorouracil?mitomycin radiosensitization.
rankedConcepts.closestError: Treat any prior chemotherapy as platinum-refractory metastatic therapy.
rankedConcepts.coverage: New standalone reflecting the 2025 FDA approval and 2026 NCI update.
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: Current treatment-line literacy matters more than memorizing unsupported doses or old regimens.

rankedConcepts.title: Oncogenic HPV causal association
rankedConcepts.decision: Distinguish the causal viral association from immunosuppression.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Anal/vulvar precursor pathology and HIV/transplant context.
rankedConcepts.closestError: Call HIV, CMV or BK the direct oncogenic association.
rankedConcepts.coverage: Four exact approved originals kept; redundant one-step coverage, no new basic acceptance.
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: Foundational biology has value, but four association variants have lower marginal yield than the new decision gaps.

rankedConcepts.title: Superficially invasive canal cancer and exact excision eligibility
rankedConcepts.decision: Decide whether a rare very-early lesion can avoid definitive CRT.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Complete excision specimen, exact depth/spread, clearance and adverse features.
rankedConcepts.closestError: Generalize every small anal-canal lesion into an excision exception.
rankedConcepts.coverage: Withheld gap; exact canal criteria need current permitted source verification and Melissa.
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: Potentially testable but exact histologic eligibility cannot be improvised.

proposals.objective: Obtain representative tissue from a suspicious anal-canal lesion before interpreting a benign outside specimen as clearance.
proposals.task: Which sampling procedure should the clinic arrange now for Evelyn Marsh’s bleeding anal lesion?

exhibit.caption: Constructed clinic teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Clinic examination
items.value: A firm, friable mass occupies the left lateral anal canal. A separate soft skin tag lies posterior to the anal verge.

items.label: Outside procedure map
items.value: The excised specimen is labelled posterior perianal skin tag.

items.label: Histology
items.value: The skin-tag specimen contains benign keratinized squamous epithelium and fibrous tissue.

choices.label: Anoscopy-guided biopsy of the canal mass
choices.rationale: The benign posterior skin specimen does not represent the left canal mass. Obtain tissue from the unresolved lesion.
choices.temptation: Use the benign finding locally while checking which lesion was sampled.
choices.counterfactual: A concerning posterior skin lesion would instead justify targeted posterior skin sampling.

choices.label: Anal cytology with HPV genotyping
choices.rationale: A screening swab does not establish histology of this firm visible lesion.
choices.temptation: Choose a less invasive HPV assessment after seeing benign tissue.
choices.counterfactual: Anal cytology can screen an eligible asymptomatic person with HIV rather than diagnose a mass.

choices.label: Deeper sections of the outside tissue block
choices.rationale: Additional sections can reassess the submitted skin tissue but cannot sample the separate canal mass.
choices.temptation: Look for missed cancer in the existing block without reconciling its anatomic target.
choices.counterfactual: If the block represented the suspicious lesion and retained relevant deeper tissue, additional sections could clarify an initially nondiagnostic sample.

proposals.explanation: The benign histology belongs to a different target. Obtain representative tissue from the canal mass; subsequent cancer staging depends on its diagnosis.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKey: Covered the key across header and specimen map. No field calls the mass cancer or says it was not sampled. Two anatomic targets replace the named omission; all options acquire or process diagnostic specimens and the key is not uniquely qualified.
manualAuthorGate.sameDecisionStageAndCategory: Three diagnostic specimen approaches: acquire lesion tissue, repeat screening, or process existing tissue; no treatment foil.
reasoningSteps: Assign the benign report to the posterior skin specimen, separate from the left canal mass.
Choose tissue from the unexplained lesion rather than screening or deeper sections of a different target.
manualAuthorGate.closestError: Treating benign tissue from one site as exclusion of disease at another palpable site.
manualAuthorGate.decidingObservation: Procedure map and current examination identify different anatomic lesions.
manualAuthorGate.consequence: A wrong-site interpretation delays diagnosis of the canal mass.
manualAuthorGate.residentDifficulty: Moderate PGY-2/3 prediction from specimen provenance and screening-versus-diagnostic sampling; not measured or independently passed.
manualAuthorGate.singleDefensibleBestAnswer: Direct biopsy of the accessible unexplained mass resolves the current histology among the offered samples.
manualAuthorGate.counterfactual: If the submitted block represented the suspicious lesion and contained unexamined relevant deeper tissue, additional sections could reasonably clarify its diagnosis; that is not the current wrong-target record.
deletionTest: Deleting the specimen map removes the basis for locating the benign result.
Deleting the mass-versus-tag distinction makes the biopsy target ambiguous.
Name, age and short clinic frame are required patient context, not key discriminators.
manualAuthorGate.sequenceReview: First node. Neither later histology nor staging is visible. Feedback gives no later nodal classification or treatment regimen.
manualAuthorGate.repairAndRecheck: Removed the already-ordered keyed workup and explicit missing-biopsy sentence. Final attack rejected repeat sampling of a soft benign tag as too weak; replaced it with credible deeper-block review and re-solved the target mismatch. All three diagnostic paths have estimates.

proposals.objective: Distinguish completed distant staging from a usable local-staging assessment before treatment planning.
proposals.currentUpdate: Biopsy of Evelyn’s canal mass now shows invasive squamous carcinoma.
proposals.task: Which step should the clinic arrange next to complete Evelyn Marsh’s pelvic staging review before treatment planning?

exhibit.caption: Constructed clinic teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Diagnostic CT chest, abdomen and pelvis
items.value: No distant lesion is identified. The interface between the anal mass and posterior vaginal wall is indistinct.

items.label: MRI acquisition log
items.value: Dedicated pelvic T2 and diffusion series were completed. The archive contains the full series.

items.label: Transferred MRI media
items.value: Contains scout/localizer images. No diagnostic pelvic series appears on the transferred media.

choices.label: Specialist review of the archived pelvic MRI
choices.rationale: Local anatomy remains a planning question, but the diagnostic acquisition exists. Obtain and review it rather than equate incomplete transfer with an unperformed scan.
choices.temptation: Reconcile acquisition, storage and transferred-series records.
choices.counterfactual: If the examination ended after localizers and the archive had no diagnostic series, dedicated MRI acquisition would be needed.

choices.label: Repeat dedicated pelvic MRI acquisition
choices.rationale: The completed diagnostic series is retained in the archive; the current limitation is the transferred media.
choices.temptation: Infer that missing exported series were never acquired.
choices.counterfactual: A technically incomplete or nondiagnostic original examination would justify a new acquisition.

choices.label: Obtain a new FDG PET/CT acquisition
choices.rationale: Metabolic staging can complement standard studies but does not replace the acquired anatomic assessment of this interface.
choices.temptation: Substitute a new whole-body study for resolution of local anatomy.
choices.counterfactual: An unresolved nodal or distant distribution question can justify complementary metabolic assessment.

proposals.explanation: Local anatomy matters despite CT without distant disease. The full pelvic MRI was acquired and retained; transfer and specialist review resolve the current information gap without repeating acquisition.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKey: The task does not name a missing test. Two options share MRI and pelvic wording, so modality matching cannot select the key. All plans have timing proposals, including specialist review; no unique wait exemption cues the answer.
manualAuthorGate.sameDecisionStageAndCategory: Three imaging-assessment steps: review an existing acquisition, repeat it, or acquire a different modality.
reasoningSteps: Recognize an unresolved local tumor–vaginal interface despite completed distant CT assessment.
Distinguish missing exported series from an unperformed acquisition and use the retained diagnostic examination.
manualAuthorGate.closestError: Repeat MRI because the referral media contains only localizers.
manualAuthorGate.decidingObservation: The scanner log and archive confirm completed diagnostic pelvic series.
manualAuthorGate.consequence: Misreading transfer status adds unnecessary testing or leaves planning anatomy unresolved.
manualAuthorGate.residentDifficulty: Moderate to hard PGY-2/3 prediction from local-versus-distant scope plus acquisition-versus-export evidence.
manualAuthorGate.singleDefensibleBestAnswer: The needed local acquisition exists in the archive, so obtaining specialist review is the justified next step.
manualAuthorGate.counterfactual: If the log showed an examination stopped after localizers and no diagnostic series existed, repeat dedicated MRI becomes best.
deletionTest: Without the log/archive rows retrieval cannot be ranked against repeat scanning.
Without the CT interface finding the local anatomic planning consequence is less explicit.
The media row establishes the actual information failure rather than an author conclusion.
manualAuthorGate.sequenceReview: Prior feedback only resolves tissue provenance. This feedback does not name inguinal staging or the next treatment answer.
manualAuthorGate.repairAndRecheck: Removed the old hip radiograph and the statement that local staging is missing. Re-solved separate acquisition/archive/export observations; preserve the original N3 construct, not its held v2 treatment identity.

proposals.objective: Select initial treatment after interpreting inguinal involvement as regional anal-cancer disease.
proposals.task: Which initial cancer treatment should be offered to Evelyn Marsh on the basis of these completed findings?

exhibit.caption: Constructed clinic teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Biopsy
items.value: Invasive squamous carcinoma from the anal-canal mass.

items.label: Pelvic MRI
items.value: A 4.2-cm canal primary involves the sphincter complex. Bladder, urethra and vaginal walls are separate from the mass.

items.label: Left inguinal-node FNA
items.value: Squamous carcinoma matching the canal primary.

items.label: Diagnostic CT chest, abdomen and pelvis
items.value: No other metastatic site identified.

choices.label: Radiation with concurrent fluorouracil and mitomycin
choices.rationale: An involved inguinal node is regional disease. This untreated canal primary remains on a curative chemoradiation pathway.
choices.temptation: Integrate nodal geography and histology before choosing treatment intent.
choices.counterfactual: Disseminated distant disease would shift the main pathway toward systemic treatment.

choices.label: Retifanlimab with carboplatin and paclitaxel
choices.rationale: This systemic option addresses inoperable recurrent or metastatic disease; the involved inguinal node does not establish distant spread.
choices.temptation: Call a node outside the mesorectum a distant metastasis.
choices.counterfactual: Multiple biopsy-confirmed distant metastases without prior platinum would support a first-line systemic regimen.

choices.label: Primary abdominoperineal resection with colostomy
choices.rationale: Sphincter involvement in this newly treated squamous primary does not create the post-chemoradiation failure indication for APR.
choices.temptation: Import a rectal-resection rule or treat sphincter invasion as an automatic operation indication.
choices.counterfactual: Confirmed resectable isolated canal recurrence after definitive chemoradiation can support salvage APR.

proposals.explanation: Inguinal spread is regional for anal SCC. A canal squamous primary without distant disease is treated with definitive chemoradiation using an established concurrent regimen; nodal positivity does not itself require a metastatic pathway or primary APR.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKey: Raw site and sampling results replace a supplied nonmetastatic stage label. No lead-in term uniquely matches one plan. Each option is a real named cancer treatment; no alone/individualized or explanatory qualifier.
manualAuthorGate.sameDecisionStageAndCategory: Three initial cancer-treatment pathways with shared background care.
reasoningSteps: Classify the sampled inguinal node as regional and retain the anal-canal squamous identity.

choices.rationale: This systemic option addresses inoperable recurrent or metastatic disease. The confined failure has a standard potentially curative local salvage pathway.

choices.counterfactual: Inoperable pelvic recurrence or disseminated metastases supports systemic oncology planning.

assertions.text: Obtain representative tissue from a suspicious anal-canal lesion before interpreting a benign outside specimen as clearance.
The benign histology belongs to a different target. Obtain representative tissue from the canal mass; subsequent cancer staging depends on its diagnosis.
The benign posterior skin specimen does not represent the left canal mass. Obtain tissue from the unresolved lesion.
A concerning posterior skin lesion would instead justify targeted posterior skin sampling.
A screening swab does not establish histology of this firm visible lesion.
Anal cytology can screen an eligible asymptomatic person with HIV rather than diagnose a mass.
Additional sections can reassess the submitted skin tissue but cannot sample the separate canal mass.
If the block represented the suspicious lesion and retained relevant deeper tissue, additional sections could clarify an initially nondiagnostic sample.

assertions.text: Distinguish completed distant staging from a usable local-staging assessment before treatment planning.

Local anatomy matters despite CT without distant disease. The full pelvic MRI was acquired and retained; transfer and specialist review resolve the current information gap without repeating acquisition.
Local anatomy remains a planning question, but the diagnostic acquisition exists. Obtain and review it rather than equate incomplete transfer with an unperformed scan.
If the examination ended after localizers and the archive had no diagnostic series, dedicated MRI acquisition would be needed.
The completed diagnostic series is retained in the archive; the current limitation is the transferred media.
A technically incomplete or nondiagnostic original examination would justify a new acquisition.
Metabolic staging can complement standard studies but does not replace the acquired anatomic assessment of this interface.
An unresolved nodal or distant distribution question can justify complementary metabolic assessment.

assertions.text: Select initial treatment after interpreting inguinal involvement as regional anal-cancer disease.

Inguinal spread is regional for anal SCC. A canal squamous primary without distant disease is treated with definitive chemoradiation using an established concurrent regimen; nodal positivity does not itself require a metastatic pathway or primary APR.
An involved inguinal node is regional disease. This untreated canal primary remains on a curative chemoradiation pathway.
Disseminated distant disease would shift the main pathway toward systemic treatment.
This systemic option addresses inoperable recurrent or metastatic disease; the involved inguinal node does not establish distant spread.
Multiple biopsy-confirmed distant metastases without prior platinum would support a first-line systemic regimen.
Sphincter involvement in this newly treated squamous primary does not create the post-chemoradiation failure indication for APR.
Confirmed resectable isolated canal recurrence after definitive chemoradiation can support salvage APR.

assertions.text: Use HRA-directed tissue assessment after abnormal anal cytology despite normal palpation in an adult with HIV.
The swab and palpation answer different questions. Abnormal cytologic screening requires HRA-directed histologic assessment; a nonpalpable lesion can still be present.
Cytology detects abnormal cells but does not supply tissue architecture. HRA identifies and samples flat lesions that need not be palpable.
If representative tissue already showed invasive cancer and local extent were unresolved, pelvic staging MRI would fit the next task.
Another swab does not resolve this high-grade screening result with histology.
Cytology can be used to screen an eligible asymptomatic person rather than replace evaluation of an already high-grade result.
The swab has not established invasive cancer; MRI does not replace lesion histology at this stage.
Biopsy-established anal cancer requiring primary and pelvic-node assessment supports pelvic MRI.

assertions.text: Treat biopsy-established anal HSIL in an adult with HIV rather than infer that virologic control removes its importance.

Intact epithelial boundaries and represented stroma distinguish HSIL from invasive cancer. Treat these lesions despite virologic suppression; electrocautery is a supported option, not a proven superior modality.
The represented disease is intraepithelial. Treating HSIL in adults with HIV reduces cancer progression; electrocautery is a reasonable option for these accessible lesions.
An unbiopsied indurated lesion would require tissue assessment before ablation.
Monitoring was a real competing strategy, but current HIV guidance recommends treatment of biopsy-confirmed HSIL. Virologic suppression does not replace lesion care.
Ongoing HRA surveillance is appropriate after successful lesion treatment.
The tissue shows intraepithelial disease rather than an invasive canal cancer; cancer chemoradiation would overtreat the represented lesions.
Representative tissue showing invasive anal-canal SCC with appropriate staging supports a cancer chemoradiation pathway.

assertions.text: Reassess a new palpable anal lesion after HSIL treatment despite a reassuring screening swab.
The new lesion changes screening follow-up into a diagnostic problem. Obtain tissue despite the negative swab; treatment of different flat lesions does not settle this finding.
A negative screening swab does not establish the histology of a new suspicious palpable lesion. Sample the current target.
With representative biopsy-confirmed SCC and unresolved local extent, MRI becomes a next-stage investigation.
Another screening specimen does not diagnose this new indurated nodule.
Screening belongs in asymptomatic surveillance when there is no suspicious current lesion.
MRI can define extent later but does not replace tissue evaluation of the new lesion.
After tissue confirms invasive disease, pelvic MRI can inform local staging.

assertions.text: Select regional salvage for isolated inguinal recurrence using primary-site status and prior radiation coverage.
Recurrence geography matters. Nodal failure in a previously treated groin with primary-site control supports inguinal dissection planning rather than automatic repeat groin chemoradiation or APR.
The active target is an isolated node in a previously irradiated groin. Regional dissection addresses that target rather than removing a controlled primary.
With no previous groin irradiation, chemoradiation to that region could become reasonable.
APR addresses local primary-site failure; the active target here is inguinal and the canal primary remains controlled.
Biopsy-proven isolated resectable canal-primary recurrence supports APR.
The original field included this groin. Selected reirradiation remains specialist work; the offered standard salvage for an isolated operable irradiated nodal target is dissection.
An isolated inguinal recurrence in an unirradiated groin can be treated with chemoradiation.

assertions.text: Select initial metastatic systemic treatment without misclassifying earlier radiosensitizing chemotherapy as platinum-refractory treatment.

Her earlier chemoradiation did not include platinum or treat this disseminated recurrence. Retifanlimab with carboplatin–paclitaxel is a supported first-line systemic option; monotherapy concerns platinum progression or intolerance.
This is initial systemic treatment of disseminated recurrence, not progression on platinum. The combination has a current US first-line indication in this setting.
Progression on or intolerance to platinum can instead support retifanlimab monotherapy.
The stated history does not meet the post-platinum progression/intolerance context. Prior fluorouracil–mitomycin chemoradiation is not platinum-refractory metastatic therapy.
Progression on platinum-based treatment or platinum intolerance supports the approved monotherapy indication.
This imports the prior radiosensitizing drugs as the systemic plan for disseminated recurrence.
Concurrent fluorouracil and mitomycin with radiation remains established for an appropriate untreated nonmetastatic primary.

assertions.text: Choose postoperative care for a small anal-margin SCC using site, differentiation and clearance rather than a blanket canal pathway.

The small skin-based, well-differentiated, node-negative SCC has generous negative clearance. Use surveillance rather than automatically treating it as a canal primary; no minimum margin cutoff is taught.
The small well-differentiated skin-based tumor has generous negative clearance and no nodal disease; further immediate cancer treatment is not required among these options.
Poorly differentiated histology with the same site and clearance would favor the offered chemoradiation plan.
Clearance is already generous and negative. More local resection does not address the actual treatment boundary in this record.
Gross residual disease or an involved edge creates a new clearance issue. The precise re-excision-versus-adjuvant ranking is held for clinical adjudication, not taught here.
This adds treatment beyond the represented favorable, adequately excised skin-margin lesion; canal origin or an adverse histologic feature would change the judgment.
The same lesion with poorly differentiated histology favors this cancer-treatment pathway.

With biopsy-confirmed recurrence and undefined local extent, MRI becomes the next staging step.
The dedicated diagnostic examination already leaves viability uncertain; repeating it does not provide histology of this accessible target.

reviewRows.title: Biopsy target after benign tissue from another site
clarityIssues: The task asks for a 'sampling procedure', but 'Deeper sections of the outside tissue block' processes an existing sample rather than sampling the patient. This category mismatch partially eliminates a distractor before clinical reasoning.

cues.phrase: A separate soft skin tag lies posterior to the anal verge.
cues.why: Together with the specimen label, 'separate' makes the wrong-target problem explicit. A reader can match the remaining mass to the only choice naming that mass without interpreting the histology. The anatomic distinction is necessary, but this option set does not make its interpretation demanding.

cues.phrase: Anoscopy-guided biopsy of the canal mass
cues.why: Only this option repeats the unresolved 'canal'/'mass' target. The two other choices concern a swab or the already benign block; the key wins by target matching.

fairness: Scope for this entire report: all 12 proposed executable nodes were reviewed using their candidate presentation, update, exhibit, task, option labels and explanation, with earlier candidate feedback considered for sequence effects. Four kept originals, seven retirement/replacement source records and two unkeyed holds were noted but not adjudicated. Review-only answer ordering and markers were not treated as cues. No statistics items occur.

This is an offline editorial review, not clinical approval or a fresh evidence verification. Difficulty and high-yield flags are qualitative judgments, not measured performance or verified exam frequencies. Every draft remains needs_clinician_review pending Melissa Rowland's exact-version sign-off.

Biopsy of the actual canal mass is the single defensible best choice among these options. Benign tissue from a different site neither excludes cancer in this mass nor makes another swab diagnostic. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
The first node is self-contained and the patient, age, sex and site are consistent. Its explanation appropriately precedes cancer staging and does not reveal the later regional-node treatment answer.
Representative tissue and screening-versus-diagnosis are high-yield concepts, but the deliberately distinct mass and soft tag reduce the purported two steps to an obvious target match.
suggestions: Use a neutral complete task asking which diagnostic step to arrange, so tissue acquisition and review of existing tissue can compete fairly.

For a resident-level item, replace the plainly unrelated benign-tag foil with a supported specimen-adequacy or target-localization problem in which reviewing existing tissue and obtaining new tissue are initially credible; give the exact specimen observations that resolve that choice. Preserve the distinction between tissue represented and tissue actually sampled.
If retaining this straightforward wrong-site safety lesson, seek explicit basic-recognition acceptance rather than labeling it moderate two-step reasoning.

reviewRows.title: Retrieving an already acquired pelvic MRI

cues.phrase: The archive contains the full series.
cues.why: Directly supplies the location and completeness of the information needed by 'Specialist review of the archived pelvic MRI'. Retrieval beats repeating acquisition by ordinary reading, without knowledge of anal-cancer staging.

cues.phrase: No diagnostic pelvic series appears on the transferred media.
cues.why: Explicitly names a transfer omission, immediately after affirming completed acquisition. The only option addressing that named omission is review of the archive.

cues.phrase: pelvic staging review
cues.why: The task's 'review' also matches the sole review option; both alternatives request a new acquisition. The key is uniquely the nonduplicative information-retrieval plan.

fairness: Reviewing the existing diagnostic MRI is a reasonable single best next step. The acquisition log correctly distinguishes missing transferred images from a scan that was never acquired. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

PET/CT can serve a different staging purpose, so feedback should not imply it has no role. It does not resolve this explicitly stated missing-MRI-review problem better than retrieving the existing series.

The biopsy update follows the preceding node coherently and supplies the diagnosis if this node is encountered independently. The subsequent MRI result can reasonably clarify the indeterminate CT interface.

Deleting the CT findings would leave the same answer. The assessed decision is chiefly record retrieval; the high-yield local-versus-distant staging distinction is background rather than a consequential inference.
suggestions: Choose whether this is an explicitly basic record-retrieval exercise or an anal-cancer staging item; do not claim both levels of reasoning.

For the staging objective, present completed studies and the specific unresolved clinical question, then compare credible investigations at the same stage. Make the actual local-extent finding change the next action instead of stating that a completed diagnostic series awaits review.
Do not repair the cue by simply hiding whether the MRI was acquired or available; that would make retrieval versus repetition ambiguous.

reviewRows.title: Regional inguinal disease and definitive initial treatment
fairness: The resident must classify inguinal spread as regional, then select definitive chemoradiation rather than a disseminated-disease regimen or primary APR. Sphincter involvement supplies a credible surgical misconception without making APR correct.

Concurrent radiation, fluorouracil and mitomycin is a defensible single best initial treatment among these options for the stated anal-canal SCC without distant disease. No confident clinical inaccuracy or equally good distractor identified.

A known histologic diagnosis is appropriate for this treatment task. 'No other metastatic site identified' does not label the inguinal node as distant; the learner still has to classify its geography. The necessary negative distant workup should remain.
Options are specific treatment plans with no meaningful length, grammar, absolute, explanatory-label or convergence giveaway. Choosing the radiation option requires medical knowledge.

The MRI resolves the prior CT uncertainty about the vaginal interface. Histology, site, nodal result and distant assessment are repeated locally, so the node stands alone. Earlier feedback supplies no regional-node classification or regimen.
This is a core surgery-board distinction with moderate predicted difficulty; no evidence supports calling its difficulty measured.
suggestions: No required editorial change. Preserve the nodal location, histology and distant-disease assessment, and keep the regional-versus-distant interpretation after answering.

reviewRows.title: Histologic evaluation after abnormal anal cytology

cues.phrase: no anal tissue specimen submitted
cues.why: Names the missing action. Only 'High-resolution anoscopy with directed biopsies' supplies tissue; the reader need not interpret the particular cytologic abnormality to identify that option.

cues.phrase: Repeat anal cytology and HPV testing
cues.why: Repeats both tests already presented as completed and abnormal. Against an MRI labeled for staging and a tissue-acquisition option, it makes simple diagnostic-sequence elimination easy.

fairness: HRA with directed biopsies is the defensible next investigation for this high-grade screening result. A normal digital examination does not clear the abnormal cytology. No confident clinical inaccuracy or competing best answer identified.

The explanation's broad phrase 'Abnormal cytologic screening requires HRA-directed histologic assessment' should stay anchored to this high-grade result; it is not a complete algorithm for every possible cytology/HPV combination.

The named 48-year-old man with HIV, screening context and task are clear and self-contained. The sequence into histology and lesion management is coherent; this explanation does not disclose the treatment key.

Abnormal-screen follow-up is useful high-yield content, but this is a single familiar escalation rule. 'No palpable anal lesion' does not create a substantial second inference against these weak alternatives.
suggestions: Delete the explicit missing-tissue sentence; retain the actual screening result and examination findings.

To retain a resident-level scored node, supply a supported, genuinely competing interpretation of the completed evaluation, such as documented targeting or sampling adequacy, and compare credible next diagnostic actions. Do not manufacture difficulty by adding unsupported screening cutoffs.
Alternatively designate this as foundational screening follow-up and obtain explicit basic-item acceptance.
Make the explanation refer to this high-grade cytology result rather than appearing to prescribe one pathway for all abnormal anal screening.

reviewRows.title: Treating biopsy-confirmed noninvasive high-grade lesions
fairness: The resident must interpret full-thickness atypia with intact basement membrane and sampled stroma free of invasive nests, then choose treatment rather than monitoring despite virologic suppression. Those are consequential histologic and management distinctions.

HRA-guided electrocautery is a defensible best choice among the three options. Monitoring represents a credible management error; invasive-cancer chemoradiation overcalls the stated tissue findings. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The lack of invasive nests in represented tissue is necessary for fairness, not an expendable cue. 'Two accessible flat epithelial lesions' is a relevant procedural observation. The explanation properly avoids claiming electrocautery is superior to all other HSIL treatments.

'Lesion-directed management' can encompass the offered monitoring plan and does not explicitly say treatment is mandatory. The options have no decisive nonmedical phrase match, outlier or convergence shortcut.

The HRA/biopsy results follow the prior investigation coherently. The current exhibit plus the patient presentation supply the necessary histology and HIV context independently. Prior feedback teaches acquisition of histology, not this treatment choice.
Recognition and treatment of HSIL in an adult with HIV is a relevant colorectal prevention concept. Difficulty is moderate rather than hard.
suggestions: No required editorial change. Preserve the actual negative invasion observation and the distinction between adequate HIV control and management of the epithelial lesions.

reviewRows.title: New suspicious nodule despite negative cytology

cues.phrase: Anoscopy with directed biopsy of the nodule
cues.why: Only this option names the task's 'new anal nodule'. The other options are the same repeat-screening and staging-MRI alternatives already rejected in the first node.

cues.phrase: The swab and palpation answer different questions.
cues.why: This exact earlier-node explanation preteaches why swab results do not settle a tissue lesion. Returning the same biopsy-versus-swab-versus-MRI choice mostly rehearses that distinction.

cues.phrase: the present nodule is a new finding
cues.why: Repeats 'New indurated ulcerated anal-canal nodule' and 'new focal pain'. The repeated novelty reinforces the targeted-nodule choice rather than adding decision information.

fairness: Directed biopsy is the defensible best investigation. Negative cytology does not exclude malignancy in a clinically suspicious nodule, and MRI does not replace tissue diagnosis. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The six-month interval is a case observation, not a universal threshold for biopsy. The change from treated flat lesions to a new painful indurated nodule is coherent and independently stated; this is not an unexplained change of lesion.

The original screening-review presentation is historical by this node, but the update makes the current visit intelligible. A new standalone presentation could be shorter and more current without changing the clinical decision.

This is a high-yield diagnostic safety principle. In this exact sequence it is easy recognition with repeated answer structure, not a fresh two-step resident problem; negative cytology adds a plausible error but not enough competition to overcome the scaffold.
suggestions: Retain the suspicious examination and negative swab; do not hide red flags to create difficulty. Remove the repeated assertion that the nodule is new.

Give this follow-up a distinct supported decision, such as choosing between credible tissue-sampling approaches when targeting or depth actually matters, with the observations needed to distinguish them. Do not reuse the first node's biopsy-versus-screening-versus-MRI set.

If the intended objective remains simply biopsy despite a negative screen, request basic-recognition acceptance or merge it into unscored follow-up teaching rather than claiming another independent moderate item.

reviewRows.title: Salvage of isolated recurrence in a previously irradiated groin
fairness: The resident must localize failure to a groin node rather than the controlled primary, then account for prior groin irradiation when choosing local salvage. The radiation-plan observation materially distinguishes surgery from a radiation-naive nodal pathway.

Right inguinal dissection is a defensible best option for this isolated mobile biopsy-confirmed recurrence among the offered plans. APR does not address an isolated groin target. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

Reirradiation can be a specialized individualized consideration; prior radiation should not be taught as an absolute ban. The current explanation appropriately says the findings support dissection planning rather than 'automatic' repeat chemoradiation. This review does not establish an exact dose, dissection extent or universal salvage rule.

Both dissection and groin chemoradiation name the right groin, so target-word matching cannot choose between them. The negative primary-site and distant assessments are needed to establish this salvage setting, not removable distractor-specific padding.

This standalone case supplies the original diagnosis, prior treatment field, current histology and restaging. It tests a useful surgical salvage distinction, although less ubiquitous than initial anal-SCC chemoradiation or salvage APR.
suggestions: No required editorial change. Preserve the prior radiation-field information and qualified multidisciplinary planning language; do not turn the answer into a categorical prohibition of every reirradiation approach.

reviewRows.title: Systemic treatment line after prior radiosensitizing chemotherapy
fairness: The clinically relevant distinction is whether previous fluorouracil/mitomycin with radiation constitutes the platinum-treated advanced-disease setting for checkpoint monotherapy. The resident must interpret that history, then choose the combination appropriate to an initial systemic line for disseminated recurrence.

Retifanlimab with carboplatin/paclitaxel is a defensible intended best option; prior radiosensitization is not synonymous with progression on platinum therapy. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. This offline review does not independently verify the current indication, jurisdictional availability or drug-label exceptions; the exact regimen still needs clinician verification.

The multiple bilateral visceral sites establish disseminated disease rather than a local salvage problem. Independence in daily activities is useful function context, not proof of every chemotherapy or immunotherapy eligibility criterion. No supplied fact establishes a contraindication or platinum intolerance that would make monotherapy equally appropriate.

The longest option is the combination, but the names are inherently longer and the other two choices do not mechanically converge on it. Word matching cannot distinguish combination treatment from monotherapy without knowing the treatment-line rule. The repeated old fluorouracil/mitomycin regimen is the weakest distractor.

The case stands alone with relevant diagnosis, distribution and prior therapy. General metastatic-versus-local treatment intent is high yield; the exact newer retifanlimab combination/monotherapy indication distinction is narrower medical-oncology detail. I would not count this exact node as established commonly tested core ABSITE coverage.
suggestions: No required editorial wording change. Treat this as supplemental current systemic-therapy coverage rather than evidence that a core surgical board concept has been covered at hard difficulty.

At clinical sign-off, verify the exact contemporary line-of-therapy indication and the explanation's progression/intolerance wording. Do not generalize the option to every patient regardless of treatment eligibility.

reviewRows.title: Surveillance after favorable anal-margin SCC excision
fairness: The resident must integrate site, small size, differentiation, lack of adverse histology and clearance to recognize a favorable local-excision situation, then choose surveillance rather than treating every anal SCC with chemoradiation or performing further excision.

Surveillance is a defensible single best option among those offered. The explicitly generous negative margin makes wider re-excision a weaker choice without requiring a disputed close-margin boundary. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The task's 'anal-margin' label supplies anatomy but does not by itself establish suitability for surveillance. Grade, extent, nodal status and excision findings still matter. Those observations should not be deleted merely because they favor the correct plan.

The 12-mm clearance is an observed fictional specimen value, not an authored universal threshold. The explanation does not assert an exact cutoff. Neither all-negative findings nor shorter surveillance wording produces a medically reliable nonknowledge shortcut: one still must know the excision exception.

The standalone case is clear and internally consistent. It is a core canal-versus-margin management concept, moderate toward the easy end for residents familiar with the exception. The separate poor-grade sibling is not earlier visible feedback for this case.
suggestions: No required editorial change. Optionally remove the post-answer author-facing aside 'no minimum margin cutoff is taught' and keep the explanation focused on the patient's eligibility and surveillance plan.

reviewRows.title: Poor differentiation after complete anal-margin excision
clarityIssues: The task is understandable, but the treatment choice does not say whether chemoradiation is postoperative adjuvant treatment. With the tumor already excised and 12-mm clear margins, that distinction matters to the claim being taught.
fairness: The resident can identify poor differentiation as an adverse feature despite small size and generous clearance, then consider treatment escalation. That is potentially a consequential two-step application and the option wording does not disclose the key nonmedically.

Unresolved clinical ranking: exclusion from a favorable local-excision pathway does not, by itself, demonstrate that this exact already-completely-excised patient must receive postoperative fluorouracil/mitomycin chemoradiation rather than surveillance. The explanation asserts the transition without establishing the postoperative recommendation. I cannot independently certify that exact ranking from these visible fields and an offline review.

This is not a confident declaration that chemoradiation is wrong, nor that surveillance is definitely equivalent. It is a specific uncertainty about postoperative management after wide negative clearance that needs exact-case clinician adjudication before the key can be independently accepted.

Wider re-excision is not a persuasive way to correct poor differentiation when the supplied clearance is already generous. The meaningful competition is surveillance versus additional oncologic therapy; the explanation should resolve that competition directly with an applicable supported recommendation.

The case stands alone and coherently differs from the favorable sibling by grade. Grade-sensitive selection is high yield, but uncertainty about the postoperative recommendation must not be counted as legitimate hard-item difficulty.
suggestions: Have Melissa adjudicate the exact postoperative scenario and verify a recommendation applicable to a small, node-negative, poorly differentiated anal-margin SCC already excised with wide negative margins. Do not treat a general exclusion from initial local-excision eligibility as sufficient proof of the exact adjuvant regimen.

If the postoperative choice is supported, explicitly label the chemoradiation plan as postoperative/adjuvant and explain why observation is inferior despite complete clearance, retaining any evidence limitation.

If that ranking cannot be supported, change the scenario to an initial-treatment decision before definitive excision, with supported findings distinguishing local excision from chemoradiation, or leave this particular postoperative question unkeyed. Do not invent a margin cutoff.

reviewRows.title: Tissue diagnosis of a new nodule in a treated scar

cues.phrase: Dedicated diagnostic T2 and diffusion images show focal scar-site thickening.
cues.why: The distractor 'Repeat pelvic MRI with diffusion imaging' repeats the specifically completed study without any acquisition problem or interval change. It is a disposable repeat-test foil.

cues.phrase: Anoscopy-guided biopsy of the scar nodule
cues.why: Only this option directly names the new nodule in the task and examination. Combined with an explicitly nondiagnostic MRI, the set strongly advertises targeted tissue acquisition.

cues.phrase: Obtain histology before selecting radical salvage treatment.
cues.why: This is legitimate post-answer teaching for the current investigation, but 'radical salvage treatment' previews the next node's only radical surgical salvage option. It is a sequence cue, not leakage into the current answer.

fairness: Biopsy is the defensible next diagnostic investigation. The late new bleeding nodule after a documented complete response warrants confirmation; indeterminate imaging is not proof of recurrence. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

PET/CT can have a restaging role, but it does not replace histologic confirmation of an accessible suspicious local lesion. The wording should preserve that distinction rather than imply PET/CT is never appropriate.

The initial node is self-contained, and the subsequent positive biopsy follows coherently. The original 18-month timing and prior flat scar differentiate this case from an early, still-regressing post-treatment lesion without inventing a response cutoff.

Biopsy before radical salvage is high yield, but the options make this an easy 'obtain tissue after indeterminate imaging' rule. The chronology is appropriate context; it does not make the repeat-MRI distractor competitive or create a robust second reasoning step.
suggestions: Remove the repeat-diffusion-MRI foil unless an actual new adequacy or interval issue makes repetition clinically credible; any such issue must be explicitly supplied and supported.

For the next-node explanation boundary, end with a neutral diagnostic rationale such as obtaining histology to distinguish recurrence from treatment-related change; do not preview radical salvage treatment.

If no distinct difficult diagnostic decision remains, use confirmation as an unscored transition into the salvage case or request explicit basic-item acceptance. Do not introduce the held early-response timing controversy merely to make this item harder.

reviewRows.title: Salvage treatment for resectable isolated local failure

cues.phrase: Obtain histology before selecting radical salvage treatment.
cues.why: The preceding node's explanation has already announced radical salvage as the coming treatment direction. The new positive biopsy now unlocks the sole operation, 'Salvage abdominoperineal resection', without requiring a fresh choice of treatment intent.

cues.phrase: confirmed local failure
cues.why: The task supplies a classification the staging findings could otherwise require the learner to establish. Alongside the prior radical-salvage scaffold, it further weakens the disseminated-disease treatment competitor.

fairness: Salvage APR is a defensible best plan among the choices for biopsy-confirmed isolated anal-canal recurrence after definitive chemoradiation with described resection planes. No confident clinical inaccuracy or equally good offered alternative identified.

Preserved planes and negative distant assessment support consideration of resection; independence in daily activities is useful context but not a complete preoperative fitness determination. The explanation appropriately recommends multidisciplinary planning rather than declaring an operation already fully cleared.
The biopsy, prior treatment and restaging are all present, so this node is clinically self-contained. The later MRI extent is compatible with the earlier scar-site finding; the sequence is coherent.

Judged independently without the prior explanation, this could be a moderate two-step application of disease distribution/resectability and salvage treatment. In the actual supplied sequence, the earlier feedback and current task supply too much of that inference; difficulty and twoStep here reflect the encountered sequence.

Salvage APR versus further definitive chemoradiation or metastatic systemic therapy is a core high-yield surgery-board decision. Its current weakness is instructional leakage, not an incorrect treatment key.
suggestions: Revise the preceding confirmation-node explanation to teach the need for tissue without naming radical salvage. This is required to repair the encountered item even though the leak resides in a companion node.

Ask neutrally which cancer-treatment plan to recommend for Maria's anal-canal cancer, letting the biopsy, treatment history, extent and distant assessment establish whether the problem is isolated local failure.

Retain the actual resection-plane and distant-disease findings. Re-review the repaired complete sequence before claiming moderate two-step difficulty; do not hide necessary staging information or label this exact version independently passed.

choices.label: Anoscopy-guided biopsy of the canal mass

choices.temptation: Use the benign finding locally while checking which lesion was sampled.
choices.counterfactual: A concerning posterior skin lesion would instead justify targeted posterior skin sampling.

choices.label: Anal cytology with HPV genotyping

choices.temptation: Choose a less invasive HPV assessment after seeing benign tissue.
choices.counterfactual: Anal cytology can screen an eligible asymptomatic person with HIV rather than diagnose a mass.

choices.temptation: Look for missed cancer in the existing block without reconciling its anatomic target.
choices.counterfactual: If the block represented the suspicious lesion and retained relevant deeper tissue, additional sections could clarify an initially nondiagnostic sample.

proposals.explanation: The benign histology belongs to a different target. Obtain representative tissue from the canal mass; subsequent cancer staging depends on its diagnosis.

items.label: Clinic examination
items.value: A firm anal-wall nodule lies beneath a shallow left-lateral ulcer and bleeds with contact.

items.label: Outside procedure map
items.value: Forceps biopsies were taken from the left-lateral ulcer edge.

items.label: Histology
items.value: Squamous epithelial strips show high-grade atypia. No connective tissue is present on the examined levels.

items.label: Block inventory
items.value: The remaining embedded material consists of epithelial strips.

choices.label: Anoscopy-guided incisional biopsy
choices.rationale: The biopsy sampled the correct surface site but contains no tissue that characterizes the underlying firm nodule. Obtain representative lesion architecture rather than infer that epithelial dysplasia excludes invasion.
choices.temptation: Reconcile the sampled layers with the palpable abnormality before selecting how to obtain diagnostic tissue.
choices.counterfactual: If the block contained unexamined connective tissue representing the nodule, specialist deeper-level review could clarify invasion without a new acquisition.

choices.label: Specialist review with additional block sections
choices.rationale: Additional sections can reassess the submitted epithelium but cannot create unsampled underlying tissue. The block inventory does not supply the nodule's architecture.
choices.temptation: Treat a correct surface biopsy location as proof that the clinically important deeper tissue is in the block.
choices.counterfactual: This is reasonable when retained tissue actually includes the unresolved lesion compartment and further sections can evaluate it.

choices.label: Repeat anal cytology with HPV testing
choices.rationale: A swab cannot supply tissue architecture of this palpable lesion or settle whether its deeper tissue is invasive.
choices.temptation: Use a less invasive epithelial test to resolve a question about underlying lesion architecture.
choices.counterfactual: Anal cytology can be used for appropriate asymptomatic screening rather than as the diagnostic endpoint for a palpable nodule.

revisedProposals.explanation: The sampled site is correct, but represented tissue matters as well as location. Epithelial atypia does not characterize the firm underlying nodule; obtain representative tissue rather than use extra levels of epithelial material as proof about invasion.

choices.counterfactual: A diagnostic uncertainty within a representative biopsy of the actual unresolved lesion can justify specialist slide review.

statementMappings.constructedBasis: Original finite fictional observations, specimen maps and chronology. No new probability, clinical cutoff, dose, regimen schedule or diagnostic duration is invented.

assertions.text: Select initial treatment after interpreting inguinal involvement as regional anal-cancer disease.

Inguinal spread is regional for anal SCC. A canal squamous primary without distant disease is treated with definitive chemoradiation using an established concurrent regimen; nodal positivity does not itself require a metastatic pathway or primary APR.
An involved inguinal node is regional disease. This untreated canal primary remains on a curative chemoradiation pathway.
Disseminated distant disease would shift the main pathway toward systemic treatment.
This systemic option addresses inoperable recurrent or metastatic disease; the involved inguinal node does not establish distant spread.
Multiple biopsy-confirmed distant metastases without prior platinum would support a first-line systemic regimen.
Sphincter involvement in this newly treated squamous primary does not create the post-chemoradiation failure indication for APR.
Confirmed resectable isolated canal recurrence after definitive chemoradiation can support salvage APR.

statementMappings.constructedBasis: Original finite fictional observations, specimen maps and chronology. No new probability, clinical cutoff, dose, regimen schedule or diagnostic duration is invented.

assertions.text: Treat biopsy-established anal HSIL in an adult with HIV rather than infer that virologic control removes its importance.

Intact epithelial boundaries and represented stroma distinguish HSIL from invasive cancer. Treat these lesions despite virologic suppression; electrocautery is a supported option, not a proven superior modality.
The represented disease is intraepithelial. Treating HSIL in adults with HIV reduces cancer progression; electrocautery is a reasonable option for these accessible lesions.
An unbiopsied indurated lesion would require tissue assessment before ablation.
Monitoring was a real competing strategy, but current HIV guidance recommends treatment of biopsy-confirmed HSIL. Virologic suppression does not replace lesion care.
Ongoing HRA surveillance is appropriate after successful lesion treatment.
The tissue shows intraepithelial disease rather than an invasive canal cancer; cancer chemoradiation would overtreat the represented lesions.
Representative tissue showing invasive anal-canal SCC with appropriate staging supports a cancer chemoradiation pathway.

statementMappings.constructedBasis: Original finite fictional observations, specimen maps and chronology. No new probability, clinical cutoff, dose, regimen schedule or diagnostic duration is invented.

assertions.text: Select regional salvage for isolated inguinal recurrence using primary-site status and prior radiation coverage.
Recurrence geography matters. Nodal failure in a previously treated groin with primary-site control supports inguinal dissection planning rather than automatic repeat groin chemoradiation or APR.
The active target is an isolated node in a previously irradiated groin. Regional dissection addresses that target rather than removing a controlled primary.
With no previous groin irradiation, chemoradiation to that region could become reasonable.
APR addresses local primary-site failure; the active target here is inguinal and the canal primary remains controlled.
Biopsy-proven isolated resectable canal-primary recurrence supports APR.
The original field included this groin. Selected reirradiation remains specialist work; the offered standard salvage for an isolated operable irradiated nodal target is dissection.
An isolated inguinal recurrence in an unirradiated groin can be treated with chemoradiation.

statementMappings.constructedBasis: Original finite fictional observations, specimen maps and chronology. No new probability, clinical cutoff, dose, regimen schedule or diagnostic duration is invented.

assertions.text: Select initial metastatic systemic treatment without misclassifying earlier radiosensitizing chemotherapy as platinum-refractory treatment.

Her earlier chemoradiation did not include platinum or treat this disseminated recurrence. Retifanlimab with carboplatin–paclitaxel is a supported first-line systemic option; monotherapy concerns platinum progression or intolerance.
This is initial systemic treatment of disseminated recurrence, not progression on platinum. The combination has a current US first-line indication in this setting.
Progression on or intolerance to platinum can instead support retifanlimab monotherapy.
The stated history does not meet the post-platinum progression/intolerance context. Prior fluorouracil–mitomycin chemoradiation is not platinum-refractory metastatic therapy.
Progression on platinum-based treatment or platinum intolerance supports the approved monotherapy indication.
This imports the prior radiosensitizing drugs as the systemic plan for disseminated recurrence.
Concurrent fluorouracil and mitomycin with radiation remains established for an appropriate untreated nonmetastatic primary.

statementMappings.constructedBasis: Original finite fictional observations, specimen maps and chronology. No new probability, clinical cutoff, dose, regimen schedule or diagnostic duration is invented.

assertions.text: Choose postoperative care for a small anal-margin SCC using site, differentiation and clearance rather than a blanket canal pathway.

The small skin-based, well-differentiated, node-negative SCC has generous negative clearance. Use surveillance rather than automatically treating it as a canal primary; no minimum margin cutoff is taught.
The small well-differentiated skin-based tumor has generous negative clearance and no nodal disease; further immediate cancer treatment is not required among these options.
Poorly differentiated histology with the same site and clearance would favor the offered chemoradiation plan.
Clearance is already generous and negative. More local resection does not address the actual treatment boundary in this record.
Gross residual disease or an involved edge creates a new clearance issue. The precise re-excision-versus-adjuvant ranking is held for clinical adjudication, not taught here.
This adds treatment beyond the represented favorable, adequately excised skin-margin lesion; canal origin or an adverse histologic feature would change the judgment.
The same lesion with poorly differentiated histology favors this cancer-treatment pathway.

assertions.text: Interpret represented biopsy architecture before deciding between additional block sections and new lesion tissue.

The sampled site is correct, but represented tissue matters as well as location. Epithelial atypia does not characterize the firm underlying nodule; obtain representative tissue rather than use extra levels of epithelial material as proof about invasion.

The biopsy sampled the correct surface site but contains no tissue that characterizes the underlying firm nodule. Obtain representative lesion architecture rather than infer that epithelial dysplasia excludes invasion.
If the block contained unexamined connective tissue representing the nodule, specialist deeper-level review could clarify invasion without a new acquisition.
Additional sections can reassess the submitted epithelium but cannot create unsampled underlying tissue. The block inventory does not supply the nodule's architecture.
This is reasonable when retained tissue actually includes the unresolved lesion compartment and further sections can evaluate it.
A swab cannot supply tissue architecture of this palpable lesion or settle whether its deeper tissue is invasive.
Anal cytology can be used for appropriate asymptomatic screening rather than as the diagnostic endpoint for a palpable nodule.

Ultrasound can assess selected local lesions, but canal narrowing limits probe-based assessment and its coverage is less comprehensive for the represented pelvic extent question.
For a small nonstenotic lesion when MRI cannot be obtained, endoanal ultrasound is a reasonable local-assessment alternative.
Metabolic staging can supplement the workup, but the current unresolved question concerns a specific local soft-tissue interface rather than a demonstrated systemic distribution gap.
An unresolved nodal or distant distribution question after appropriate local assessment can justify complementary PET/CT.

The low-grade skin-wart specimen does not resolve high-grade cells in an anal swab. HRA more precisely delineates flat epithelial lesions that a normal palpation or standard white-light examination can miss.
If high-grade cells were traced to a fully assessed represented lesion and the unresolved issue were its slide interpretation, targeted pathology review could be appropriate instead.
Repeating white-light assessment does not provide HRA's more precise delineation of potential flat lesions behind the discordant high-grade screen.
When HRA is unavailable, standard anoscopy with biopsy of identified lesions is a supported pathway, with its scope made explicit.
Review can refine the submitted skin diagnosis but does not inspect the anal epithelium that produced the high-grade screening cells.
A diagnostic uncertainty within a representative biopsy of the actual unresolved lesion can justify specialist slide review.

A small well-differentiated node-negative skin-margin lesion amenable to negative-margin excision can instead be considered for local excision.
Small size, skin location and absent nodes make this tempting, but poor differentiation defeats the favorable local-excision selection in this scenario.
With well-differentiated histology and otherwise suitable small node-negative skin-based disease, local excision is a supported option.
An adverse differentiation result is not itself a reason for primary APR of this nonmetastatic skin-margin tumor. Radical resection has a different role in appropriate local failure after treatment.

passPreservation.routingNote: The legacy middle HSIL node becomes final. Existing reviewed rationales are reused in neutral no_terminal_outcome routing required by schema. No scored or visible clinical field changed.

clarityIssues.issue: The task asks for a 'sampling procedure', but 'Deeper sections of the outside tissue block' processes an existing sample rather than sampling the patient. This category mismatch partially eliminates a distractor before clinical reasoning.
clarityIssues.response: The task now asks which diagnostic step to arrange, so acquisition and processing of retained tissue are both valid categories.

cues.phrase: A separate soft skin tag lies posterior to the anal verge.
cues.originalConcern: Together with the specimen label, 'separate' makes the wrong-target problem explicit. A reader can match the remaining mass to the only choice naming that mass without interpreting the histology. The anatomic distinction is necessary, but this option set does not make its interpretation demanding.
cues.response: Removed the separate soft skin tag; the biopsy is from the clinically correct site, leaving specimen layers rather than obvious anatomic mismatch as the problem.

cues.phrase: Anoscopy-guided biopsy of the canal mass
cues.originalConcern: Only this option repeats the unresolved 'canal'/'mass' target. The two other choices concern a swab or the already benign block; the key wins by target matching.
cues.response: No option repeats canal mass as a unique target label. Incisional biopsy competes with deeper-block review until the epithelial-only inventory is interpreted.

issueResponses.fairnessDisposition: Retains the representative-tissue principle while requiring interpretation of high-grade epithelium versus unrepresented invasion. No biopsy depth threshold or technique hierarchy is invented.
issueResponses.suggestionDisposition: Used a matched-target specimen-adequacy problem and a neutral task. The rubric records a block-inventory counterfactual; no basic-recognition acceptance is claimed.
issueResponses.sourceNotes: Claims and source-to-question mappings are in the revised statement mappings and source ledger.

cues.phrase: The archive contains the full series.
cues.originalConcern: Directly supplies the location and completeness of the information needed by 'Specialist review of the archived pelvic MRI'. Retrieval beats repeating acquisition by ordinary reading, without knowledge of anal-cancer staging.
cues.response: Removed the complete archive and record-retrieval key. The current specimen, CT interface and canal findings create a clinical imaging decision.

cues.phrase: No diagnostic pelvic series appears on the transferred media.
cues.originalConcern: Explicitly names a transfer omission, immediately after affirming completed acquisition. The only option addressing that named omission is review of the archive.
cues.response: Removed the transfer-media omission rather than hiding whether a scan was acquired; this new scenario does not ask retrieval versus repetition.

cues.phrase: pelvic staging review
cues.originalConcern: The task's 'review' also matches the sole review option; both alternatives request a new acquisition. The key is uniquely the nonduplicative information-retrieval plan.
cues.response: Removed pelvic staging review and all sole-review option wording. All options are actual staging acquisitions.

issueResponses.fairnessDisposition: PET remains a complementary staging investigation. CT local interface and examination now drive local extent and acquisition scope; this is not an administrative task with decorative CT findings.
issueResponses.suggestionDisposition: Compared MRI, endoanal ultrasound and PET/CT using local anatomy and stenosis. The ultrasound limitation is supported by a rights-checked imaging review, with current society support for MRI local staging.
issueResponses.sourceNotes: Claims and source-to-question mappings are in the revised statement mappings and source ledger.

cues.response: Deleted no anal tissue specimen submitted. The actual submitted skin-wart specimen and standard examination are shown instead.

cues.response: Removed repeat-swab and staging-MRI alternatives. Two procedures now acquire directed biopsies; interpretation requires specimen compartment and acquisition scope.

issueResponses.fairnessDisposition: Feedback explicitly applies to this high-grade anal result, not every abnormal screening combination. Normal palpation and a low-grade perianal wart are not treated as clearance of the anal epithelium.
